title: Odysseus's Wife Recognised the Beggar as Her Husband Early — She Just Didn't Say So
dek: The hosts argue Penelope recognised her disguised husband long before the reveal: her uncharacteristic laughter, her reading of her son's sneeze as an omen of the suitors' deaths, and her talk of proper bride-gifts are all signals — and Odysseus understood them.
why: A low-density book-by-book close read, but the debate over whether Penelope had already recognised her husband, and the setup of putting everyone in one house as a moral test, are useful to anyone writing about revenge and the return to power.
who: People who have read the Odyssey or are catching up on it; screenwriters and novelists writing narratives of revenge, disguise, and the transfer of family power.
skip: The last two minutes, on Nolan not being able to shoot comedy.

points.h: The one recognition that needs no deception
points.body: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, enters the city and passes Argos, the old dog lying in the mule dung with no one to tend him. The dog wags his tail, his ears droop, and Odysseus weeps but cannot go over and hold him — the goatherd Melanthius is right there, and any exposure would destroy the revenge plan. The hosts say this passage is special because the book is layered with deception everywhere: deceiving his mother, deceiving his most loyal slave woman, whereas with Argos there is only pure perception, cutting straight across, requiring no testing at all. One student wrote a paper arguing Argos is Ithaca itself: a place neglected, slowly rotting, with no one stepping in to fix it; the suitors are the dung, and both Argos and Telemachus lie in the dung without becoming dung.

points.h: Has she actually recognised her husband or not
points.body: One host says this is the book's biggest hermeneutic question, one he has worn everyone out with in his honors college class: by the end of Book 18, has Penelope recognised Odysseus? The other host's answer: if you don't ask, I'd say no, the text reads as if she hasn't; but once you ask, I think she has. The evidence: a fugitive prophet brings an oracle saying he is already on Ithaca; Telemachus sneezes, and she laughs, calling it an omen of the suitors' deaths — before this she was either crying or about to cry her bed wet, never this happy. The counter-evidence comes from the same person: Telemachus earlier wouldn't bring her before Odysseus, because over the years many people had come bearing good news, all of them lying. The two land on this: she is already winking at her husband in Greek Morse code.

points.h: This character test doesn't decide who dies
points.body: Athena has Odysseus disguised as a beggar begging among the suitors, to see who is good and who is bad — but the text says immediately afterward that she had no intention of saving anyone in the slaughter that follows. So the character test in this house carries no survival payoff; even the consistently friendly Amphinomus dies all the same. The hosts say this is a reminder: the point of the test is not to decide who lives. They attribute the test's motive to Athena — what she wants is to draw out Odysseus's bloodlust, to get him back into a killing state, not to sift out who deserves pardon.

points.h: Begging in your own house is the hardest self-control
points.body: One line gets repeated throughout the disguise: a beggar cannot have shame. Odysseus has to behave in the most shameless way possible, and the hosts think this is harder than taking the stool to the back or enduring Melanthius's abuse — a once-great king now begging in his own house, from these people, for food that is rightfully his. The humiliation is close to the limit here, but the more accurate word is that it humbles him: he is pressed down to the lowest point, in some sense he brought it on himself, and by accepting it and owning it he is rebuilding his personhood out of it. There's another layer: as king he was always courteous to beggars, and now that he is one, he might even feel some relief — finally knowing what those people's lives were like.

points.h: Winning is fine, winning too beautifully gives you away
points.body: Another farce is Irus — a fat drunk who serves as the suitors' messenger, hence the nickname Iris — coming to fight Odysseus over begging territory, with the two of them set up to box and the prize a goat's stomach stuffed with fat and blood. The hosts say Odysseus is walking a tightrope: he can't possibly be beaten by this drunk, but he also can't hit too hard, because once the other suitors step in to help, he'll have to beat them all too and his identity blows up on the spot. So his trick is to make them swear that no one will lift a hand for Irus. The hosts compare it to Clark Kent fighting an ordinary person: you can't show your real strength. Another laugh: the moment Irus shows fear, Antinous turns on him instantly, saying he'll ship him off to some king who cuts off people's noses and ears.

points.h: The one who's really haunted is Odysseus himself
points.body: After winning, Odysseus sits down beside Amphinomus and delivers that speech: of all creatures that live and breathe and crawl on the earth, man is the weakest; our mood depends on whatever Zeus sends each day. Then he warns him: don't turn from the right path, don't disrespect the wife of a man who will soon be home. Amphinomus understands, paces back and forth in the house, his heart stirred — the hosts say this is where they start reading these books as a ghost story: Odysseus comes back to town like High Plains Drifter, letting the suitors reveal their true faces and dig their own graves. But he adds that maybe he is the ghost, and he himself seems haunted by something too. The narrator's closing is cold: the good get no exemption, and Amphinomus still has to die on a spear.

points.h: Penelope starts playing her own hand
points.body: Athena first gives Penelope a makeover, making her more beautiful and raising desire in the suitors' hearts. One host says he sometimes leans toward reading it as metaphor: a person who for so long could only weave the shroud and unravel it, weave and unravel, keeping the clock stopped, decides to act for the first time, and that excitement is itself the light on her face. The other won't give up the literal sense: the storyteller most likely really believed a god did this. Right after, Penelope tells the suitors that her husband made her promise to remarry once her son grew a beard, and the date has come; but a respectable family courting should bring fat sheep and cattle and good gifts, not eat another man's food for free. Odysseus is pleased to hear it, because her mouth is saying fine words while her mind is calculating something else — the hosts wonder how he can be so sure this is a ploy when he hasn't tested her yet. Their answer is domestic: a husband just knows when his wife is speaking from the heart.

points.h: The god wants Odysseus to ache inside
points.body: After the slave woman Melantho taunts him and Eurymachus leads the mockery, the text says Athena keeps the suitors provoking him, wanting the pain to sink deep into Odysseus's heart. The hosts ask why: one intuition is that she wants to stir up righteous anger; another is that it's both — she enjoys a good fight, and Odysseus hasn't been in a warrior's mindset for a long time. This passage also makes them notice that the gods may not actually need to intervene: these people have been drinking all day and have seen so many strange things, they can go that mad on their own, no god needed to teach them to do vile things. And in these books Athena is very active yet never appears as she once did, so even the hosts can't say for sure whether Odysseus and Telemachus know she's pulling strings.
